Medieval Music. The musical traditions of Europe from roughly the sixth to the fifteenth centuries, a period defined by the dominance of the Catholic Church in musical life. Spanning from single-voiced Gregorian chant to complex polyphonic motets, medieval composers developed the notation systems and harmonic principles that would underpin all European concert music. The era reflects a world where sacred music was virtually synonymous with serious composition.

Medieval music began with Gregorian chant, also called plainchant, monophonic Latin liturgical singing organized in modes rather than major or minor tonality. Pope Gregory the First is traditionally credited as the nominal source of the Gregorian tradition, though modern scholars debate the attribution.

Medieval music gradually incorporated polyphony. By the twelfth century, parallel voices singing different lines emerged, called organum, leading to the motet. The motet became the highest art form: a sacred polyphonic form in which each voice sang different Latin texts simultaneously, creating harmonic density.

Composers like Josquin des Prez and Palestrina perfected Renaissance polyphony, which grew from medieval foundations. Hildegard of Bingen, a twelfth-century German nun and visionary, composed liturgical chants and texts that survive as rare examples of female medieval authorship.

The development of musical notation allowed composers to specify exactly which notes to sing, revolutionizing the transmission of music. Medieval churches became the first concert halls. The acoustics of cathedrals became an essential part of composers' creative vocabulary. The modes used in medieval music, Ionian, Dorian, Phrygian, and Lydian, provided the organizational system from which Western tonality later evolved.

Gregorian chant is the foundational monophonic tradition of medieval liturgy. Hildegard of Bingen is a medieval composer and mystic whose works survive in manuscript. The motet is the apex of medieval polyphonic form. Polyphony is the structural innovation that defined later medieval music. Plainchant is an alternative term for the chant tradition central to medieval practice. Renaissance music is the successor period, growing directly from medieval polyphonic sophistication. The Catholic liturgy is the institutional context that preserved and promoted medieval music.
